title: Start the Next Project Immediately
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece advises creative and knowledge workers to begin outlining or sketching their next project immediately after finishing the last one, rather than taking a break first, as a way to prevent the paralysis of starting cold. It explains the mechanism as leveraging both the emotional high of recent completion and the momentum of skills and habits still actively engaged, arguing that a pause of even a few days makes restarting noticeably harder. The piece is careful to note the recommended sequence isn't 'no rest' — practitioners can and should still take a break, just after the rough outline of the next project already exists. It closes with a quoted maxim about the value of simply getting started.
points: Starting the next project immediately after finishing the last one is framed as a way to leverage both post-completion euphoria and still-active momentum.
The recommended sequence is to sketch a rough outline first, then take a break — not to skip rest altogether.
A pause of more than a few days is described as making restarting noticeably more painful, likened to detraining physical conditioning.
Sustained continuity is argued to reduce downtime costs and let recent learnings carry forward directly into the next effort.
quotes: Staring at a blank screen or piece of paper is among the most painful of creative challenges. Inertia and writer’s block between assignments can affect even the most skilled practitioners.
That’s why so many writers, artists, and performers advise practitioners to start the next project immediately after finishing the last one.
Once the new project has been started, the practitioner can now take a break and allow the brain to rest, recharge, and incubate new ideas.
Creativity muscles and conditioning are much like physical ones. Breaking off from the work for more than a few days makes starting again painful and slow.
As a wise person once said, “The secret of getting ahead is getting started.
